@@60971663 <p> Staging a major sailing event which best reflects the spirit of your beloved home port is not a challenge for the faint-hearted writes W M Nixon . When we consider the multiple factors involved in the completion of the complex four-day programme for the O'Leary Life Sovereign 's Cup 2019 which concluded in Kinsale this afternoon , we soon realise that people like Regatta Director Bobby Nash and KYC Commodore David O'Sullivan and their voluntary and varied team of supporters in their many roles are quietly setting an example which could be usefully transferred to many aspects of local and national life , both afloat and ashore . <p> Yet it 's in the nature of such people that they see the need for something to be done , and they just get on and do it . Central to it is the willingness to take on board lessons from previous stagings of this biennial classic , while at the same time observing any fresh innovations which may have proven effective in major events elsewhere , and taking them on board for incorporation into the Kinsale model . <p> The view to the sea over Kinsale -- the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ organisers of an event for a very varied fleet . <p> Kinsale 's shoreside charms are such that a successful regatta will seek to provide good racing within a civilised timeframe each day <p> But that 's not as simple as it sounds . Characterful and hospitable Kinsale with its beautiful natural harbour is in many ways in a league of its own as a sailing venue . The Sovereign 's Cup programme has to be designed in such a way that its staging is in harmony with the civilised mood of this multi-functional centre of the good life . In other words , the people involved in staging the Sovereign 's Cup learn more from their own biennial running of this highly individualistic regatta than they do from looking elsewhere , and a critical self-analysis after each Sovereign 's regatta is part of their approach . <p> So it was that despite June 2019 being one of the busiest sailing periods ever seen in Ireland ( with Kinsale getting its own early share with the invasion at the beginning of the month by the 50th Anniversary Figaro fleet ) @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ neatly filed away , and Kinsale ready and waiting for the O'Leary Life Sovereign 's Cup 2019 with a fine and varied entry of 95 boats in all - Cruiser-Racers and two One Designs classes including the International Dragons in their National Championship -- facing into an interesting programme providing something for everyone . <p> Class 0 start on the first day , with Frank Whelan 's Eleuthera ( eventual overall winner by a clean sweep ) in the foreground . Photo : Robert Bateman <p> Competitors were almost spoilt for choice , with four start lines operational . Irish Sailing President Jack Roy was in charge of the top end IRC racing for Classes 0 , 1 and 2 , Neil Prendeville looked after the two white-sail divisions ( W1 and W2 ) , Richard Leonard oversaw each day 's single Coastal Race which was favoured by mostly larger boats , and the two hot One Designs -- the International Dragons with their Irish Nationals , and the 1720s with their Europeans - were in the competent hands of Peter Crowley . <p> The Dragons in full cry , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ The Dragon Gold Cup will be staged at Kinsale in 2020 . Photo : Robert Bateman <p> More so than ever -- or so it seemed - it was the weather which had the final say . In times past , we lived with the possibly mistaken assumption that our weather progressed in a reasonably orderly fashion , coming in from the Atlantic and heading towards us in a regular and predictable manner mainly from the southwest and west in a way which usually provides sailable conditions each day , such that often on the south coast , the old clich ? about " champagne sailing " can be trotted out at some stage . <p> But we 're living in an era of climate change , and far from Kinsale being comfortably located in a line of useful Atlantic-based sailing weather , the approach of weather systems from several directions -- with some of them freakish such as the Continental heat-wave -- resulted in Kinsale itself being at the heart of a meteorological innovation and manufacturing unit at Sovereign 's Cup time . <p> While it may be stretching @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , the 1720s were very pleased to get clear visibility and enough wind for decent racing . Photo : Robert Bateman <p> Thus although the opening day on Wednesday saw everything off to a cracking start with a good easterly , most weather predictions were suggesting that Thursday would be a non-racing day with Mistral-like easterly gales . And so it proved . In fact , national wind charts and data suggested that the strongest winds in all Ireland were funnelling right through the racing area off Kinsale . <p> One of the explanations for all this was that Ireland 's western seaboard from West Cork north to Donegal was experiencing the hottest weather in the entire island . Thus , where mountains loomed large , the rising hot air accelerated the wind blowing towards them . For frustrated crews in Kinsale , the explanations became ever more exotic , and one comment on the message lines was that the easterly gale cutting through Kinsale was entirely the fault of excessive temperatures on Ireland 's biggest mountain , Carrauntoohill in Kerry ... <p> Former Kinsale YC Commodore John Twomey had @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a Blazer 23 . A variant by Laser designer Bruce Kirby on the popular Sonar , the Blazer was built in Canada by Ontario Yachts with the American MORC ( Midget Ocean Racing Club ) circuit in mind . John 's crew in Kinsale included Eugene Hinkel , who made the original moulds in Oakville , Canada , and subsequently in Florida used Shillelagh as his demo boat before selling her to an owner in Tampa . In time , he arranged for her re-sale to the renowned Kinsale skipper , and personally looked after the boat 's shipment to Ireland . Photo : Bob Bateman <p> As ever , the sagacious John Twomey , Paralympic Sailing superstar and former Kinsale YC Commodore , was to put it back in perspective with a wry comment : " The weather is the boss " , and left it at that while going out next day to continue his successful regatta in the Blazer 23 Shillelagh . With the weather frontal systems - which had removed the easterly gale and brought the fog - shifting and evaporating ever so slowly to the eastward , there was just the chance that a nice south to southwest wind might develop , and seldom can weather predictions have been dissected with as much thoroughness as they were last night in Kinsale . <p> Despite a contretemps in Friday @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Outrajeous ( Richard Colwell &amp; Johnny Murphy ) regained her composure and a discard and a win in the final race today and finished tops overall in IRC 2 . This heat tends to diffuse inside until it escapes through the surface of the earth 's crust . <p> This energy would be enough to cover the world 's needs if it could be used , but geothermal energy is an energy that is difficult to use . <p> The temperature is distributed irregularly according to the zones of the earth 's crust . The bags of magma that come from the deeper areas move towards areas of lower pressure . <p> At its contact , the rocks melt , and it releases large amounts of gases that tend to escape through cracks and fissures in the crust , giving rise to volcanic phenomena such as volcanic eruptions , high-temperature gas outputs , hot water outlets ( hot springs ) , etc. although only some of these are usable . <p> Man has been using geothermal energy since remote times . I believe a more apt name would be moderately-paced charger . I pulled in expecting a quick 20-minute top up , but that was not the case and ended up taking more like 50 minutes . <h> ' THE GOAL FOR IRELAND IS TO GET 950,000 EVs BY 2030 <p> HERE the Irish EV Owners Association 's GUILLAUME SEGUIN lays out his blueprint for @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ country.He said : " With the Climate Action Plan 2019 , the Government is sending us a clear message -- we will all have to change our habits in order to limit climate change and its catastrophic consequences . We will have to use many levers in order to reduce our emissions . We will have to switch our fossil burning machines for EVs . " The goal is to get 950,000 EVs by 2030 and from that year onwards , each new car sold will have to be zero emissions . " This timeline may sound aggressive but 11 years is still far away at today 's world pace . Do n't forget the iPhone was created just 12 years ago . To ensure a successful transition we need three elements : a choice of cars , a solid charging infrastructure , and a change of habits . " Today there are just 14 pure EVs available on the Irish market . In a year 's time this number will double . " Infrastructure is the key element . We will quickly need a much more dense and improved @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ longer journeys . City and county councils will also have to install street chargers , companies will have to cater for employees and customers , even if we charge at home 90% of the time . " Finally , we will have to change our habits . Just like when we got our first iPhones , we will plug in our cars overnight and soon forget that 12 years ago we had Nokia phones lasting for a week on a charge . No one is traumatised by charging their phones daily . We can evolve . " <p> As I was waited patiently for the ' fast ' charger to gradually saunter along , I got chatting to a Dublin taxi driver who pulled into the adjacent bay . <p> I asked how the switch to electric was working out and he gushed about how fantastic it was , telling me in great detail how much he loved the motor . <p> He told me that the bill to power his car for the previous month was roughly the same as a full tank of gas had cost him previously @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ charge can cost as little as ? 2 using cheaper night rate electricity . <p> That is economical but looking forward , it is hard to see those prices being maintained if a quarter of the country is hooking up overnight . <p> After roughly 50 minutes I decided to make do with whatever I had -- 180km -- and head towards the airport . <p> I took the scenic route through the city and it drove like a dream -- smooth , slick , and quiet . I never noticed how much noise a traditional car made , no purring engine or vibrating exhaust . <p> From the airport I headed north towards Drogheda . Along the way I passed the M1 Lusk services which had no working fast charger . <h> HIGH SPEED DRAINS BATTERY <p> As I hit the motorway I noticed how the higher speed drained the battery and less braking also meant less battery regenerating during driving . The power-sapping air con did n't help either . <p> After reaching my destination , I turned around and head back towards the capital . En route @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ had been slashed in half . <p> To avoid a fine , I had to return the car with more than 25 per cent power , so I made a beeline for the closest charging point in Glasnevin . <p> Of course , it was out of order , so I headed back to my favourite spot in Dublin Port . <p> This is when disaster struck -- or more correctly when my dyslexia kicked into gear . <p> As I headed down East Wall Road bopping away to tunes , I was fully aware that I needed to turn right . But , I just ignored my brain and took a left turn straight into the Port Tunnel . Panic set in . I had roughly 40km worth of juice left , I obviously could n't turn around , and the Dublin Airport charging point was out of order . <p> My only option was to thump it through the tunnel -- at the speed limit -- and then pray I had enough power to whip back around . <p> That plan was swiftly derailed as the Southbound bore @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ was light and I was able to make it back to Dublin Port . After charging the car up again for another 30minutes or so I returned it from whence it came . <h> CHARGING NETWORK IS CAUSE FOR CONCERN <p> I can definitely understand the appeal of an electric car for city driving . It is perfect for navigating urban areas . <p> But for those who would be relying on it to travel long distances across the country the current charging network gives cause for concern -- which can be seen in the lack of uptake outside of big city dwellers . Revenue figures show that from 2014 to 2018 only 3,150 EVs were purchased with more than half of those registered in Dublin and Cork . <p> When you include Wicklow , Kildare , Galway and Meath , those six counties represent over 71 per cent of all EVs during that span . <p> There are a number of positive reasons to make the move to electric -- the environmental benefits , the cost benefits , and the ability to self-righteously judge those in the pollution patrol @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of tax -- ? 120 a year , reduced toll charges , and can avail of free parking in some areas across the country . But the greatest deterrent is the national charging network . The Government can incentive electric cars all it wants , but it needs to focus on creating a wide spanning , reliability , of public charging network to build motorist confidence . <h> SHOOTING HORROR <h> ROAD HORROR <p> There are sections of motorway that span 100km between ESB fast charging points . On the M9 , Naas in Kildare to Knocktopher in Kilkenny is a 108km drive , while on the M8 , Fermoy in Cork to Urlingford in Kilkenny is roughly 95km . <p> And the N3 has no fast charging point after Navan in Meath , leaving an over-70km trip to Cavan town . <p> Motorists make mistakes , they get lost , take wrong turns or miss exits . The country needs a charging infrastructure that is idiot-proof -- and I can attest to that first hand .

@@60974759 <h> Shouting louder will not defeat populism <p> A demonstrator watches a burning car near the Champs-Elysees avenue during a demonstration in December 2018 in Paris over rising taxes . Emmanuel Macron was the first national leader to enact tax cuts on the basis of where one lives . As a result , 1% of France 's GDP is now being redistributed first to the poorest parts of the country . The focus is on actions , not just elections . Picture : AP Photo/Kamil Zihnioglu <p> Monday , July 01 , 2019 - 12:00 AM <p> Decades ago , traditional governments in the West were the mainstream . Today , they are alone in the woods , wondering where everyone went , say Isma ? l Emelien and David Amiel <p> The political parties that once dominated Western democracies have been shaken to the core . <p> Many have suffered electoral debacles , not least in France , Italy , Greece , and the United Kingdom . Others have changed so radically that only their name remains the same . The Republican Party of US president , Donald Trump , has little in common with that of former @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ across the West . Leaders of the once-dominant parties oscillate between denial and despair , while populists siphon off their traditional supporters . <p> Some refuse to see any legitimate reason for their defeat , dismissing their opponents ' supporters as " deplorables , " as Hillary Clinton did shortly before losing to Trump in 2016 ; others are too petrified by the populist surge to mount a counter-offensive . <p> But neither denial nor complacency will break the political impasse . Progressives must rebuild , and that starts with diagnosing the traditional parties ' shortcomings . <p> Traditional parties failed to recognise the real issues of the age . Still fighting on old ideological battlefields , they turned a blind eye to declining social mobility , mounting environmental crises , rising geographic inequality , tensions over multiculturalism , and other issues that matter to voters . <p> Decades ago , they were the vanguard , the mainstream . Today , they are alone in the woods , wondering where everyone went . The social sciences may have an answer . The gap between their objective analysis of reality and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Western countries , for example , economists have long known about the growing divide , in terms of incomes and other indicators , between some affluent cities -- which benefit from globalisation -- and the rest of the country . <p> Yet not until French president , Emmanuel Macron 's administration did a national leader enact tax cuts on the basis of where one lives . As a result , 1% of France 's GDP is now being redistributed first to the poorest parts of the country . <p> Traditional parties could also learn something from listening to voters directly , rather than only through the filters of media and pollsters . Back in 2016 , Macron 's movement , ' En Marche ! ' , started with the largest door-to-door listening tour in France 's history . What voters told canvassers then became the foundation of Macron 's presidential campaign . <p> For example , more than a year before revelations of Hollywood film producer Harvey Weinstein 's alleged sexual predations , ' La Grande Marche ' had gathered innumerable testimonies from women about harassment , and Macron issued @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> At the time , Macron 's stance made him the butt of opponents ' jokes ; the laughter soon faded with the onset of the #MeToo era . <p> Still , an accurate understanding of society is not enough . Traditional parties also suffer from poor organisation . They have long-believed that modern politics should be organised around elections , with activists showing up periodically to hand out leaflets and cheer on the candidates . <p> This was not cynicism , so much as a symptom of an approach that treats democracy as a marketplace comprising government providers and citizen consumers . In this view , seizing and holding power is a party 's sole raison d ' ? tre . It is little wonder that citizens , and even party members , feel ignored between elections . <p> Despite these weaknesses , established parties had a number of advantages that forestalled their collapse . In recent years , they have had a technological edge over less-established opponents , and they were the only political actors with ready constituencies that could mobilise people for elections , organise protests , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ longer sustainable . Citizens nowadays refuse to be mere consumers of public policies . With rising levels of education have come new demands for empowerment . Voters want to be treated as political actors in their own right , not as pawns in someone else 's game . <p> Moreover , governments themselves are no longer the sole providers of policies . This is one of the hard lessons we learned during two years working alongside Macron at the ? lys ? e Palace . <p> The leading policy challenges today -- climate change , religious extremism , digital disruption , gender equality -- do not admit of solutions only by national governments . Such challenges demand deep cultural changes , and action at the sub- and supra-national levels . <p> Finally , technology has lowered entry barriers to political participation , such that traditional parties can no longer count on an incumbent advantage and entrenched support networks . When you have mastered Google , Twitter , and Facebook , you do n't need a century-old party machine . <p> Political movements must be rebuilt accordingly . The focus should @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ party 's formal management structure should serve as the administrative ' back office ' ; the front office should be staffed by the people on the ground . At ' La R ? publique En Marche ! ' , we refer to these as local citizen projects . <p> They can include anything from after-class reading courses and migrant integration programmes to cooperative vegetable gardens and digital training sessions for senior citizens . <p> In each case , the point is to offer solutions tailored to local problems , thereby strengthening communities . Such projects should now be regarded as essential complements to public policies . <p> In the future , a party 's ability to offer rewarding avenues for political and community engagement will be essential to its attractiveness . And by daily demonstrating progressivism in action , parties will have already laid the groundwork for success when election day arrives . <p> When voters refuse to hear what you have to say , shouting louder is not the answer . This is the hard lesson traditional parties learned . Only by demonstrating a commitment to improving lives , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to come to your side . <p> Reconnecting with voters ' concerns thus goes hand-in-hand with adapting party organisations . For a winning alternative to populism , we need grassroots progressivism . <p> Isma ? l Emelien , a co-founder of ' En Marche ! ' , has been head of strategy for French president , Emmanuel Macron , since 2014 , and was Macron 's special adviser for strategy and communication , from 2017 to 2019 . David Amiel coordinated the conception of Macron 's campaign platform and was a policy adviser to the president , from 2017 to 2019 .
